title: Trees Can Sense Their Shape and Straighten Up
paragraphs: That a tree might know the shape of its own trunk sounds like a conceit from a children's story, yet research from the French institute INRAE, published in New Phytologist, suggests precisely this. Beyond the familiar cues of light and gravity, trees appear to monitor their own curvature, and they respond with a mechanism that bears a striking resemblance to muscular action.

The experiment was elegantly spare. Young poplars were left to grow on their sides for about ten days until the stems had arched upward, then set on a slowly rotating horizontal platform inside a uniformly lit sphere, a device that dissolves consistent gravitational and luminous cues and leaves a tree with nothing to go on but its own form. Within weeks the stems had all but righted themselves. Tension wood, long assumed to be confined to the upper side of a stem, stopped forming there and emerged on the opposite flank, the two tissues pulling against each other like antagonistic muscles. Bruno Moulia, a research director at INRAE, spoke of "a genuine sensorimotor loop operating in the woody parts of trees".

Prudence is nonetheless in order. The hoped-for dividends, which include straighter timber, sturdier cereals and trees better able to recover from storms, are the authors' conjecture rather than demonstrated fact. The report gives no sample size, rests on a single young tree type in a contrived setting, and was funded by French space and agroecology bodies, which is to say that replication, not enthusiasm, will determine how far the finding travels.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'children's story' suggest about the idea at first?
questions.a: That it sounds fanciful or unlikely.

questions.q: What did the rotating platform achieve?
questions.a: It removed consistent gravity and light cues, leaving only the tree's own shape.

questions.q: Why does the writer urge prudence?
questions.a: The benefits are speculative, the sample size is missing, and the setting was artificial.
